text.p: These are tough times for the mark. A lacklustre German economy, talk of Bundesbank interest rate cuts and a drive towards European convergence have sent the mark to its lowest levels in years.
And analysts say things will get worse before they get better.
"There must be some upside somewhere but it's difficult to see what it is," said an economist at a UK bank.
The past week has seen the German currency sink to 30-month lows against the dollar and more than four-year troughs against sterling and the Norwegian and Danish crowns.
It has hit its weakest level against Finland's markka in a year and its lowest versus the Italian lira since June 1994.

Highlighting German economic woes, a newspaper reported on Friday that the government was increasingly concerned it would overshoot the strict budget deficit criteria needed to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The Bonn Finance Ministry quickly retorted that the government still expected to meet the criteria.

But Handelsblatt, quoting unnamed officials, said a public spending freeze would be imposed this month and that Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt assumed there would be 4.2 million jobless in Germany in 1997 -- 200,000 above the previous target.

"What the mark needs is some evidence that the recovery is really taking hold and we have a fairly muted view of the strength of the recovery," said Brian Hilliard, senior international economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.

"We're not looking for anything that'll be enough to reverse the rise in unemployment, which is one of the clearest symptoms of the weakness of the economy," he said, noting the harm done to consumer confidence and demand by high jobless levels.
Though the short- and medium-term outlook looks bleak, some analysts saw the economy performing better later in the year.
"Longer term we expect the mark to regain the upper hand, as German economic growth continues," said James McKay, international economist at PaineWebber.
For now, however, CIBC Wood Gundy's chief economist David Coleman said the German goal of cutting the 1997 budget deficit to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product looked less achievable by the day.
"This environment is one in which a tight monetary policy makes no sense. The scope for lower short-term interest rates is still there," Coleman said.
Market rate cut speculation was stoked on Thursday by Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp.
He said the record German jobless figures issued last week proved the economy was in a grave position. "Monetary policy cannot be indifferent to this situation," he said.

Though Krupp is seen as a Bundesbank dove, his comments attracted much market attention. Easier rates are anathema to a market already unimpressed by low German yields and whose thirst for yield seems unquenchable.
"People want the yield and they'll do whatever is necessary to get there," said Nick Douch, economic and corporate risk adviser at BZW in London.
The process of convergence ahead of monetary union is a major millstone around the mark's neck, analysts said.
"There's quite a lot of momentum towards further convergence in the European bond markets and that is supporting optimism on the European currency crosses," said PaineWebber's McKay.
The German authorities have turned a deaf ear to the mark's suffering, hoping that the dampening effect on export prices will deliver a fillip to competitiveness and the economy.

But recent central bank action -- intervention by Finland, a Spanish rate cut which failed to weaken the peseta -- is a reminder that currency strength is just as unwelcome for Germany's neighbours as they, too, struggle to boost growth.
